verified_ref: Ashtavakra Gita 18.100, the last verse of chapter 18 (same number in Nityaswarupananda's Astavakra Samhita and Jalim Singh's Hindi tika).
context: This closes the hundred-verse eighteenth chapter, in which Ashtavakra describes how the freed person lives: not excited by praise, not hurt by blame, not afraid of death (18.99). Chapter 19 then turns to Janaka, who answers with his own account of resting in the Self.

key_terms.sense: one whose mind has become quiet
a crowded place, full of people
however things are, wherever one is

core_teaching: Peace is not a matter of location. The settled person does not chase society or flee to solitude, because neither attraction nor aversion is driving the choice; they remain the same wherever life puts them.

commentaries.who: Jalim Singh, Ashtavakra Gita bhasha-tika (1903, Hindi)
commentaries.gist: The calm, freed person does not rush toward crowded places, because he has no attachment to them, nor toward the forest, because he has no aversion to people. In town or forest he stays steady and the same.

commentaries.who: Swami Nityaswarupananda, Astavakra Samhita (translation reading, no note)
commentaries.gist: Reads the verse plainly: the tranquil one runs after neither the crowd nor the wilderness and remains the same in any condition and place. He adds no separate note to this verse.

practical_reading: A reader who keeps thinking peace lies in a different place (a quieter city, a retreat, a busier social life) can use this to notice that the restlessness travels with them; the work is on the chasing, not on the address.
misreadings: Not a rule against solitude or retreats, nor against social life; it rejects running to either out of craving or aversion.
Not a description of indifference to people; Jalim Singh frames it as freedom from attachment and aversion.
cautions: Describes the state of a jivanmukta; a reader who cannot yet feel 'the same everywhere' should not read it as a judgement on themselves.
speaks_to: restlessness that keeps looking for the right place
someone torn between moving to the city and moving away from it
people who feel calm only on holiday
not_for: someone who needs to leave an unsafe home or workplace: the verse is about inner chasing, not about staying put in harm
acute loneliness, where telling the reader the crowd does not matter could feel dismissive
research_note: Both commentaries read from OCR (Ambuda proofing text; archive.org OCR of Jalim Singh). Richards' translation named in our data was not re-read here.

verified_ref: Avadhuta Gita 1.18 (same number in Paramananda's Khemraj edition and in Kannoo Mal's translation).
translation_note: 'Ghost' renders piśāca (a restless goblin or spirit); both readings checked use the image of a ghost wandering about.
context: Chapter 1 is Dattatreya's song of the one Self. In 1.14 he already asks why one runs here and there like a ghost when the Self is inside and outside; 1.15-17 say union and separation, and the five sense objects, do not belong to the Self. Here he turns to his own mind directly.

key_terms.sense: you run about confused, like a restless ghost
see the Self as not divided, not other than you

core_teaching: The mind's frantic searching comes from treating the Self as something somewhere else; seeing it as one's own undivided being, and letting go of clinging to objects, is what brings ease.

commentaries.who: Swami Paramananda, Paramanandi Hindi bhasha-tika (Advaita)
commentaries.gist: The mind roams like a ghost looking for the Self as if it were separate; that is the basic mistake. See it as non-different, drop attachment to objects, because sorrow lasts only as long as clinging does.

commentaries.who: Kannoo Mal, English translation with introduction (translation reading, no note)
commentaries.gist: Renders it as a call to the mind to stop wandering bewildered, to realise the Atma as indivisible, give up desire and be happy.

practical_reading: Teachers use it as a self-talk practice: when the mind is spinning, name it and speak to it, then ask what it is chasing and whether letting go of that one thing would bring rest.
misreadings: Not contempt for the mind or for the reader; it is the sage scolding his own mind gently.
'Drop attachment' is not 'stop caring about people'; Paramananda means clinging to sense objects as sources of happiness.
cautions: The ghost image is mild here, but for someone with intrusive thoughts or anxiety disorders, 'just drop it and be happy' can sound like blame; pair with practical steps.
speaks_to: restless searching for meaning in the next thing
someone who keeps changing plans and is tired
not_for: clinical anxiety or panic, where 'be happy' would be glib
grief in its first days

verified_ref: Numbered 1.67 in both editions checked (Paramananda's Khemraj edition and Kannoo Mal). Chapter 1 numbering differs by one across editions; our 1.68 may follow another printing.
translation_note: 'Mere speculation' renders vitarkyam ('a matter for argument'); Paramananda takes it as: the visible world is what is open to argument, while the essence already told is that you are Brahman, untouched like space.
context: Near the end of chapter 1, after many verses negating every attribute of the Self, Dattatreya stops arguing and sums up. The next verses speak of the knower dissolving into the whole like pot-space into space, wherever he dies.

key_terms.sense: the essence, the heart of it
like the sky: vast and untouched

core_teaching: After all the reasoning, the point is simple: what you are is not the chatter but the sky-like awareness in which it moves.

commentaries.who: Swami Paramananda, Paramanandi Hindi bhasha-tika (Advaita)
commentaries.gist: Dattatreya tells his own mind there is no use in more talk; the world is what is open to debate, but the settled conclusion already given is that you are pure awareness, unstained and unattached like space.

commentaries.who: Kannoo Mal, English translation with introduction (translation reading, no note)
commentaries.gist: Renders it as: what is gained by so much talk and intellectual wrangling? The real essence has been told: thou art the highest Self, unlimited like space.

practical_reading: Useful when overthinking: notice when analysis has stopped helping, return to one simple truth, and let the commentary in the head be weather in a large sky.
misreadings: Not anti-intellectual; it ends discussion only after the teaching has been given.
Not telling the reader their thoughts or worries are meaningless.
cautions: Advaita identity language ('you are reality itself') can feel abstract or alienating to someone who needs comfort; it works better as a pause than as an argument.
speaks_to: someone tired of their own inner debate
not_for: someone whose 'chatter' is a real problem needing practical decisions
people in crisis who need concrete help
research_note: Verse number: both texts read number it 1.67; flag for editor.

verified_ref: Avadhuta Gita 2.1 (same in Paramananda's edition and Kannoo Mal).
translation_note: 'Jewel fallen in dirt' renders aśucau praviṣṭam; Kannoo Mal renders it as a diamond encrusted with impurities. Same sense.
context: Chapter 2 opens with two verses on the teacher. Kannoo Mal's introduction links them to Dattatreya's well-known twenty-four gurus (earth, water, a pigeon, a prostitute, a child and others): wisdom is taken wherever it is found. The chapter then returns to the Self.
core_teaching: Judge teaching by its truth, not by the teacher's age, status, learning or lifestyle; you would not throw away a jewel because of where it was lying.

commentaries.who: Swami Paramananda, Paramanandi Hindi bhasha-tika (Advaita)
commentaries.gist: Reads 2.1 with 2.2: do not weigh whether the guru knows poetry or lexicons; take the essence a teacher has and leave the rest. A boat carries you across whether or not it is painted.

commentaries.who: Kannoo Mal, English translation with introduction (introduction)
commentaries.gist: Sums up a key piece of advice of the text: a seeker should pick up wisdom wherever he finds it, like a bee gathering honey from many flowers, never despising its source. Cites 2.1-2 and the twenty-four gurus.

practical_reading: Learn from unlikely people: a junior colleague, a child, someone whose life you would not choose. Ask 'is this true?' before 'who said it?'
misreadings: Not an endorsement of abusive or exploitative teachers; it is about not dismissing truth for superficial reasons, not about excusing harm.
Not a claim that the teacher's conduct never matters.
cautions: In a reader's life this could be misused to justify staying under a harmful guru or boss; editors should frame it as 'take the good', not 'tolerate everything'.
speaks_to: someone dismissing advice because of who gave it
not_for: someone currently in an exploitative spiritual or workplace relationship

verified_ref: Avadhuta Gita 2.2 (same in Paramananda's edition and Kannoo Mal).
translation_note: Our_note says the verse excuses the plain style of Dattatreya's own verses. Both sources read here apply it to the teacher instead: do not judge a guru by poetic skill. The reading about the text is possible but should not be stated as the only one.
context: Second of the two opening verses on teachers in chapter 2. It follows 2.1's jewel-in-the-mud image with a second image: an unpainted boat.

key_terms.sense: only the essence is to be taken
a boat without red paint or decoration

core_teaching: Substance matters more than polish. A plain boat still gets you to the other shore; a plain teacher or plain words still carry truth.

commentaries.who: Swami Paramananda, Paramanandi Hindi bhasha-tika (Advaita)
commentaries.gist: Do not judge the guru by literary accomplishment; take the essence. He adds: do not just pierce your ears and join someone's sect; become one who takes in virtues, since without knowledge and dispassion no one is freed.

commentaries.who: Kannoo Mal, English translation with introduction (introduction and translation)
commentaries.gist: Reads the verse about the guru: whether or not he has poetic learning, the wise take the good in him; a boat without vermilion painting still carries passengers across.

practical_reading: When choosing what to read, whom to listen to or how to judge your own work, ask whether it carries you across, not whether it is impressive.
misreadings: Not a dismissal of beauty or craft.
Not specifically about this app's own texts; the classical readers read it about teachers.
research_note: Our_note's reading (self-reference to the text's style) is not supported by the two sources read; flagged in notes.

verified_ref: Avadhuta Gita 2.7 (same in Paramananda's edition and Kannoo Mal).
translation_note: Our_note calls the first half (pramādena) obscure. Paramananda reads it as: I do not produce the mind's movements through negligence; Kannoo Mal similarly: do not think it is I who propel the mind's deceptive impulses. The translation's sense holds.
context: After 2.3-6 describe the Self as effortless, all-pervading and bodiless, 2.7 deals with thoughts: they are not the Self's doing. 2.8-9 follow with the image of qualities that are inseparable from their substance, as coolness is from water.

key_terms.sense: carelessness, heedlessness (read as: I do not cause them through negligence)

core_teaching: Thoughts come and go on their own like bubbles in water; the Self only witnesses them and does not need to chase, fight or own them.

commentaries.who: Swami Paramananda, Paramanandi Hindi bhasha-tika (Advaita)
commentaries.gist: The movements of the inner mind are not produced by me; like bubbles in water they rise and merge back by themselves, and I am simply their witness.

commentaries.who: Kannoo Mal, English translation with introduction (translation reading, no note)
commentaries.gist: Renders the first half as a warning not to think that it is I who drive the mind's deceptive impulses; they arise and dissolve like bubbles in a river.

practical_reading: A plain mindfulness instruction: when a thought bubbles up, notice it, do not grab it, and watch it pop.
misreadings: Not 'nothing you think or do matters' or a denial of responsibility for actions.
Not saying thoughts are bad; only that they are not who you are.
cautions: For obsessive or intrusive thoughts this can help, but 'they dissolve by themselves' is not a promise that distressing thoughts will stop quickly.
speaks_to: meditation beginners frustrated by a busy mind
not_for: someone using detachment to avoid a decision that does require action

verified_ref: Avadhuta Gita 2.24 (same in Paramananda's edition and Kannoo Mal).
context: Late in chapter 2, after verses on the knower's identity with the Self, Dattatreya names the qualities of the one who reaches the highest. The next verse compares the knower's death to a pot breaking and its space merging with space.

key_terms.sense: delighting in the good of all beings

core_teaching: Freedom is marked by three things together: no grudges or cravings, active goodwill toward every being, and a steady, settled understanding.

commentaries.who: Swami Paramananda, Paramanandi Hindi bhasha-tika (Advaita)
commentaries.gist: Only the knower who is free of attachment and aversion, wishes the good of all and the harm of none, has firm knowledge of the Self and is steady reaches the highest state; no one else does.

commentaries.who: Kannoo Mal, English translation with introduction (translation reading, no note)
commentaries.gist: Renders it as one free from passions and animosity, disposed to do good to all beings, of firm convictions and strong mind, who attains the supreme goal.

practical_reading: A short self-check for a day: what am I clinging to, whom am I resenting, and what one thing can I do for someone else's good?
misreadings: 'Free of attachment' does not mean cold; the same line asks for active care for all beings.
Not a demand to have no feelings.
cautions: Holding up 'no aversion' to someone who has been wronged can feel like being told to stop protecting themselves; the verse is about inner grudges, not about losing boundaries.
speaks_to: service-minded people who want a spiritual frame
not_for: a person in an abusive situation, where 'no aversion' could be heard as 'make peace with it'
research_note: Our_note's link to Gita 5.25 and 12.4 (sarva-bhūta-hite ratāḥ) is a well-known parallel; not re-checked in this run.

verified_ref: Avadhuta Gita 3.34 (same in Paramananda's edition and Kannoo Mal).
translation_note: The translation omits the refrain's last line, which the verse ends on: 'I am the nectar of knowledge, of one taste, vast as the sky' (jñānāmṛtaṃ samarasaṃ gaganopamo 'ham). Our setting also says Dattatreya speaks 'to a grieving friend'; Paramananda reads it as addressed to his own mind ('friend'), Kannoo Mal glosses friend as the heart. No other person is grieving in the text.
context: Chapter 3 is a long hymn whose verses end with the refrain 'I am the nectar of knowledge, of one taste, like the sky.' From 3.34 on, a run of verses asks 'Why do you weep, friend?' and lists things the Self does not have: age, death, birth, form, change.

key_terms.sense: why on earth do you weep, friend?
I am the nectar of knowledge, of one taste, sky-like

core_teaching: Weeping over ageing, death and birth belongs to identifying with the body; the Self one truly is does not age, die, get born or change.

commentaries.who: Swami Paramananda, Paramanandi Hindi bhasha-tika (Advaita)
commentaries.gist: Dattatreya speaks to his own mind: weeping out of fear of age and death is mistaken, since your nature is free of them; you were never born, so birth's pain is not yours; resolve that you are knowledge, one, all-pervading.

commentaries.who: Kannoo Mal, English translation with introduction (translation reading, no note)
commentaries.gist: Takes 'friend' as the heart; it has no birth pangs, old age, death or change, and the speaker is deathless knowledge, unchanging and all-pervading like space.

practical_reading: Some teachers use the refrain as a meditation when afraid of ageing or illness: notice what in you watches the body change and has not itself changed.
misreadings: Not a rebuke to anyone who is grieving a death.
Not a claim that the body's pain is unreal or unimportant.
cautions: Strong caution for grief: 'why do you weep?' said to a mourner can feel dismissive and shaming. Our setting ('a grieving friend') makes this worse; it should not be used on Day 1 of any grief plan.
Speaks of death and birth directly.
speaks_to: fear of one's own death, in a calm reflective moment
illness that is changing the body
not_for: fresh bereavement
someone who has just had a frightening diagnosis and needs to be heard first
children's grief
research_note: Setting text should be corrected: the address is to Dattatreya's own mind or heart, not to a grieving friend.

verified_ref: Avadhuta Gita 3.46, last verse of chapter 3 (same in Paramananda's edition and Kannoo Mal).
translation_note: Kannoo Mal construes the second line differently (the Atma is by nature immaculate and immortal) and does not call renouncing and not-renouncing 'poison'. Our rendering matches Paramananda's.
context: This closes chapter 3's long refrain-hymn. Having negated every attribute of the Self, Dattatreya ends by negating even the act of renouncing; chapter 4 opens by asking how there can be invocation or farewell, flowers or meditation, for the formless.

key_terms.sense: let go, let go of worldly life
renouncing and not renouncing: both poison

core_teaching: Letting go is the path, but holding on to the identity of 'one who has let go' is a new bondage; one's nature is already free and needs neither.

commentaries.who: Swami Paramananda, Paramanandi Hindi bhasha-tika (Advaita)
commentaries.gist: Give up the world, then give up renunciation too; know both renouncing and its absence as poison. The pride 'I am a renouncer' is itself very painful; only by dropping pride in both do you find full happiness.

commentaries.who: Kannoo Mal, English translation with introduction (translation reading, no note)
commentaries.gist: Give up the world, give up renunciation, give up both renouncing and not renouncing; the Atma is by nature spotless and immortal.

practical_reading: Watch for spiritual pride: the diet, the detox, the minimalism or the quitting can become a new identity to defend. Let that go too.
misreadings: Not permission to drop all discipline because 'renunciation is poison'; the verse comes after renunciation, not instead of it.
Not saying the world or family is poison.
cautions: 'Let go of the world' could be read by a depressed reader as withdrawal from life; the classical reading is about dropping self-image, not dropping out.
speaks_to: someone defining themselves by what they gave up
not_for: someone already withdrawing from people and duties in depression

verified_ref: Avadhuta Gita 7.9 (same in Paramananda's edition and Kannoo Mal).
translation_note: Both sources keep manasā kalpita ('formed/projected by the mind'): Paramananda says the yogi slowly moves in the natural bliss as shaped by the mind; Kannoo Mal, 'spontaneous felicity projected by the mind'. Our 'natural joy of the mind' is acceptable; our_note correctly flags the phrase as read differently.
context: Chapter 7 describes the wandering avadhuta in rhymed couplets: rags from the road, beyond merit and sin, beyond union and separation. The next verse asks how one still tied to ideas of duality or non-duality can be free.
core_teaching: The free person is not driven either to grab experiences or to refuse them; he moves through life unhurried, in a joy that does not depend on either.

commentaries.who: Swami Paramananda, Paramanandi Hindi bhasha-tika (Advaita)
commentaries.gist: The yogi absorbed in the Self is free of union and separation, of permitted and forbidden enjoyment; such a one moves slowly, slowly in natural bliss, that is, he reaches the joy of the Self.

commentaries.who: Kannoo Mal, English translation with introduction (translation reading, no note)
commentaries.gist: Renders the ascetic as one free of union and disunion, an enjoyer free of enjoyment and non-enjoyment, who gradually attains the spontaneous felicity projected by the mind.

practical_reading: Slow down: walk, eat and work at a pace that is not chasing a reward or proving a discipline.
misreadings: Not laziness or passivity.
Not a rejection of pleasure; it is freedom from both craving and refusing it.
speaks_to: all-or-nothing habits around food or pleasure
someone who wants to enjoy life without guilt or compulsion
not_for: someone struggling with addiction who needs firm abstinence, not 'neither enjoying nor refusing'

verified_ref: Avadhuta Gita 8.2; the same verse is Bhagavata Purana 11.11.30 (Krishna to Uddhava), verified on vedabase.net. Our_note's 'recalled, not verified' can now be marked verified.
attribution_note: Speaker in the Avadhuta Gita is Dattatreya; the verse is shared with the Bhagavata, where Krishna speaks it. Worth noting in the app so readers are not surprised.
translation_note: 'Has taken refuge in Me' (mac-charaṇaḥ): the Bhagavata reads it as refuge in Krishna; Paramananda, in the Advaita context of the Avadhuta Gita, reads it as refuge in the Self.
context: Chapter 8 opens with Dattatreya asking forgiveness for three 'faults' of worship (pilgrimage to the all-pervading, meditating on what is beyond thought, praising what is beyond words). Verses 2-4 then list a sage's qualities, borrowed from the Bhagavata's list of a saint's marks.

key_terms.sense: intellect not struck down by desires
taking refuge in Me / in the Self

core_teaching: A portrait of quiet strength: steadiness of mind, gentleness, purity, few needs and moderation, rooted in a single refuge.

commentaries.who: Swami Paramananda, Paramanandi Hindi bhasha-tika (Advaita)
commentaries.gist: One whose intellect is not spoiled by desire, who has mastered the outer senses, is gentle, pure, holds nothing, wants nothing, eats little, is calm, steady and speaks little: that one is a knower of the Self.

commentaries.who: Bhaktivedanta Book Trust purport to Bhagavata 11.11.29-32 (Gaudiya Vaishnava)
commentaries.gist: Treats these lines as part of a list of twenty-eight saintly qualities; following Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati it calls taking full shelter of Krishna the key one, from which the others grow.

practical_reading: Pick one quality as a day's practice: eat a little less, speak a little more gently, or let one wish go unpursued.
misreadings: Not a call to own nothing or to starve; mita-bhuk means moderate.
Not a checklist to judge oneself harshly against.
cautions: For readers with eating disorders, 'eats moderately' should not be the line a reading builds on.
not_for: readers with disordered eating
someone already feeling they fall short of every ideal

verified_ref: Avadhuta Gita 8.3; the same verse is Bhagavata Purana 11.11.31, verified on vedabase.net.
attribution_note: Shared with Bhagavata 11.11.31 (Krishna to Uddhava).
translation_note: jita-ṣaḍ-guṇa: our 'six waves' (hunger, thirst, grief, delusion, age, death) follows the Bhagavata purport. Paramananda instead takes the six as the inner enemies (desire, anger, greed, delusion, pride, envy). Either is traditional; the app should not present one as the only meaning.
context: Second of the three borrowed Bhagavata verses listing a sage's marks at the start of chapter 8, before Dattatreya explains each syllable of the word 'avadhuta'.

key_terms.sense: master of the six (waves of bodily life, or six inner enemies)
seeking no honour, giving honour to others

core_teaching: Inner depth shows outwardly as alertness, steadiness, humility that still honours others, friendliness and compassion.

commentaries.who: Swami Paramananda, Paramanandi Hindi bhasha-tika (Advaita)
commentaries.gist: Ever watchful, of deep nature, patient, having conquered the six vices (desire, anger, greed, delusion, pride, envy), without pride, skilled in all work, friendly to all and kind: such a one is called a sadhu.

commentaries.who: Bhaktivedanta Book Trust purport to Bhagavata 11.11.29-32 (Gaudiya Vaishnava)
commentaries.gist: Glosses the six as hunger, thirst, lamentation, illusion, old age and death; amānī as not puffed up even if famous; māna-da as respecting everyone as part of Krishna.

practical_reading: Give credit and respect freely today without asking for any back.
misreadings: 'Seeking no honour' is not low self-worth or accepting disrespect.
speaks_to: being kind without being a pushover
not_for: someone whose self-esteem is already crushed and who hears 'seek no honour' as 'you deserve none'

verified_ref: Avadhuta Gita 8.4; the same verse is Bhagavata Purana 11.11.29 (the first of the three), verified on vedabase.net. Note the order differs: in the Bhagavata this verse comes before the other two.
attribution_note: Shared with Bhagavata 11.11.29 (Krishna to Uddhava).
context: Third of the borrowed Bhagavata verses at the start of chapter 8. Paramananda ends his gloss with 'such am I', reading the list as the sage's self-description.

key_terms.sense: harming no one, bearing no malice

core_teaching: Compassion, harmlessness, patience with everyone, truthfulness to the core, evenness and helpfulness belong together as marks of a free person.

commentaries.who: Swami Paramananda, Paramanandi Hindi bhasha-tika (Advaita)
commentaries.gist: One who is compassionate, forbearing, bears malice to no embodied being, sees one Self everywhere, speaks only truth, is free of birth and death and helps everyone: such am I.

commentaries.who: Bhaktivedanta Book Trust purport to Bhagavata 11.11.29-32 (Gaudiya Vaishnava)
commentaries.gist: Akṛta-droha: never offensive in return even when offended; titikṣu: forgives and forgets offences against oneself; sarvopakāraka: works for others' welfare. Frames all of it as devotion to Krishna.

practical_reading: Practise one act of patience today with someone who tests you, and one act of help no one asked for.
misreadings: Titikṣā is a quality of the saint, not a demand on someone being harmed to keep putting up with it (our_note says this well).
cautions: For readers being mistreated, 'patient with all beings' must not be read as 'tolerate abuse'.
speaks_to: wanting to be a kinder person
not_for: someone in an abusive relationship
research_note: The BBT purport is copyright and includes sectarian polemic; use only for the plain glosses above.

verified_ref: Avadhuta Gita 8.6 (same in Paramananda's edition and Kannoo Mal).
context: After 8.5 says these marks should be known by all seekers, 8.6-9 explain the word a-va-dhū-ta syllable by syllable. This verse gives 'a'.

key_terms.sense: freed from the noose of hope and expectation
pure at beginning, middle and end

core_teaching: The first mark of the free person is release from the noose of expectation, which leaves a steady, clean joy.

commentaries.who: Swami Paramananda, Paramanandi Hindi bhasha-tika (Advaita)
commentaries.gist: Free of the noose of hope for pleasures of the world; pure in waking, dream and sleep, or in past, present and future, or in childhood, youth and age; always immersed in Brahman's bliss. This is the meaning of 'a'.

commentaries.who: Kannoo Mal, English translation with introduction (translation reading, no note)
commentaries.gist: The letter 'a' shows that he is free from the net of hope, free from beginning, middle and end, and always abiding in happiness.

practical_reading: Notice one expectation you are holding over a person or outcome today and loosen it; see what is left when you are not waiting for it.
misreadings: Not 'abandon hope' in the sense of despair; āśā here is craving for outcomes.
cautions: 'Free of hope' can land badly with someone depressed or hopeless; frame as freedom from clinging expectation, never as giving up.
not_for: someone who feels hopeless or suicidal

verified_ref: Avadhuta Gita 8.7 (same in Paramananda's edition and Kannoo Mal).
translation_note: 'Lives in the present' for vartamāneṣu varteta follows Paramananda (he lives on what comes in the present and does not worry about the future). Kannoo Mal reads it as 'abides in all existing things'. Our line is defensible but one reading among two.
context: Second of the four syllable-verses explaining a-va-dhū-ta: this gives 'va'. The next verse gives 'dhū' (body covered in dust, mind cleansed, beyond concentration and meditation).

key_terms.sense: speech that is healthy, causes no hurt

core_teaching: The free person has let go of old cravings, speaks in ways that do no harm, and lives in the present rather than in the future's worries.

commentaries.who: Swami Paramananda, Paramanandi Hindi bhasha-tika (Advaita)
commentaries.gist: He has dropped both good and bad latent desires, since he no longer needs even purification; his words cause no one pain; he lives on what the present brings, absorbed in joy, without worrying about the future.

commentaries.who: Kannoo Mal, English translation with introduction (translation reading, no note)
commentaries.gist: The letter 'va' shows he is bereft of desires, his speech is free of evil, and he abides in all existing things.

practical_reading: Three practices in one: drop one old craving, say nothing today that wounds, and do the task in front of you without rehearsing tomorrow.
misreadings: 'Lives in the present' is not 'make no plans'; Paramananda means not being consumed by future anxiety.
speaks_to: habits that come from old cravings

verified_ref: Dheesh (Dhisha) Gita 1.5-6 in both Bharat Dharma Mahamandal editions read (the printed numbering counts the speaker line 'suta uvaca' as 1). Our '1.4-5' is off by one.
attribution_note: Speaker Suta is correct, but he is addressing his teacher Vyasa, not 'Shaunaka and the sages'. He reports what he once heard from Vyasa and asks Vyasa to recite the Dhisha Gita.
context: The text opens with Suta thanking his guru Vyasa for the Puranas and Gitas already taught, recalling Vyasa's teaching that the Lord is called Dhisha because he presides over the intellect, and asking to hear the Gita in which Ganesha taught the seers. Vyasa then narrates.

key_terms.sense: father of the world, friend of the world
out of compassion, presiding over the intellect
tender toward those who take refuge
lord (īśa) of the intellect (dhī): a name of Ganesha

core_teaching: The divine both stands beyond the mind and, out of compassion, works through it; that is why Ganesha is called lord of the intellect and gives freedom to those who turn to him.

commentaries.who: Bharat Dharma Mahamandal Hindi bhashanuvada (publisher's own Hindi rendering; no classical commentary exists)
commentaries.gist: The Lord, beyond the intellect, out of kindness dwells in the intellect and gives liberation to beings; therefore all the Vedas call him Dhisha. Suta then asks why and how the seers reached Dhisha's world.

practical_reading: A prayer-frame for clear thinking: ask for help not only with the outcome but with the mind that will choose.
misreadings: Not a claim of Vedic origin for this text; 'the Vedas call him Dhisha' is the text's own statement.
cautions: The Dheesh (Dhisha) Gita is one of five sectarian 'Gitas' (Vishnu, Surya, Shakti, Dhisha, Shambhu) issued by the Bharat Dharma Mahamandal, Kashi. core_teaching: Learning and accomplishment did not bring peace; peace came only from turning toward the source with humility and asking to know it.

core_teaching: All life is held and fed by a sustaining order that works like a mother's care, carrying beings step by step toward freedom.

commentaries.gist: By the dharma-filled motherly nature of Ganesha's Prakriti, beings are protected and nourished without break, and so pass upward through the forms of birth to human life, where they become fit for the path to liberation.

practical_reading: A grounding thought on a hard day: you have been carried this far by more care than you can see.
misreadings: Not a promise that nothing bad will happen; the verse is cosmological.

guarding from the mass of wrong actions
may it urge toward good action
whose left side is adorned by Siddhi

core_teaching: A prayer for the mind itself: may the divine light protect it from wrong action and turn it toward the good, day and night.

commentaries.who: Bharat Dharma Mahamandal Hindi bhashanuvada (publisher's own Hindi rendering; no classical commentary exists)

practical_reading: A short morning prayer before a day of choices; can be said before work or study.
misreadings: Not a replacement for the Vedic Gayatri; it is modelled on it.
cautions: The Dheesh (Dhisha) Gita is one of five sectarian 'Gitas' (Vishnu, Surya, Shakti, Dhisha, Shambhu) issued by the Bharat Dharma Mahamandal, Kashi. austerity, self-control, truth, guarding the self
bring the pleasant and unpleasant under one's own control

core_teaching: The core work is discipline, self-restraint, truth and inner guarding, ending in untying the heart's knots so that likes and dislikes no longer rule you.

commentaries.gist: Renders the answer as penance, self-restraint, truth and subjugation of mind, untying the heart's knots and mastering the agreeable and disagreeable. Footnote (from the commentator Nilakantha): tapas is doing one's own duties; knots mean attachments and desires.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition text (12.288) as a textual check
commentaries.gist: The critical text has this verse as 12.288.7 with the same wording as ours; the swan goes on to warn at once against wounding speech (288.8-9).

practical_reading: Choose one 'knot' today, a grudge, a craving, a fear, and loosen it a little, so that a like or dislike does not decide your next action for you.
misreadings: Not about suppressing feelings; it is about not being ruled by them.

verified_ref: Mahabharata 12.288.10 (BORI critical edition, Mokshadharma, Hamsa Gita). Ganguli/Roy translation: Santi Parva section CCC (300). Our data's '12.305.10' matches neither; the verse number within the chapter (10) is correct.
attribution_note: Speaker is the Swan, who in 12.288.3 is Prajapati (the unborn, eternal creator) in the form of a golden swan; listeners are the Sadhya gods. Bhishma narrates to Yudhishthira.
translation_note: Our Sanskrit has pratihṛṣyate ('stays cheerful'), the vulgate reading Ganguli translates ('rejoices without yielding to anger'). The BORI critical text reads pratimṛṣyate ('bears it patiently'). Our English follows the vulgate; worth a note.
context: Just before, the swan warns that word-arrows fly from the mouth and wound the hearer's vitals day and night, so the wise should never shoot them (12.288.8-9). This verse turns to the other side: what to do when you are the target.

key_terms.sense: calm alone is to be practised

core_teaching: When someone attacks you with words, answer with calm; the one who stays unprovoked keeps their goodness and, in the epic's moral accounting, gains the attacker's merit.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli's translation (P. C. Roy edition, Santi Parva section CCC), with footnotes drawing on Nilakantha
commentaries.gist: If someone pierces a wise man with word-arrows, he should keep peace; one who, provoked, rejoices without yielding to anger takes away all the provoker's merit.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition text (12.288) as a textual check
commentaries.gist: Critical text 12.288.10 reads 'pratimṛṣyate' (endures) where ours reads 'pratihṛṣyate' (rejoices): the core instruction, calm under verbal attack, is the same.

practical_reading: When a message or comment stings, wait before replying; reply only from calm, or not at all.
misreadings: Not 'accept abuse silently forever'; it governs your reaction, not whether to set boundaries.
The 'merit transfer' is the epic's moral language, not a promise of revenge.
cautions: For someone being bullied or abused, 'stay cheerful' can sound like 'it's your job to absorb this'; pair with permission to step away.
not_for: victims of ongoing abuse or harassment

verified_ref: Mahabharata 12.288.11 (BORI critical edition, Mokshadharma, Hamsa Gita). Ganguli/Roy translation: Santi Parva section CCC (300). Our data's '12.305.11' matches neither; the verse number within the chapter (11) is correct.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli's translation (P. C. Roy edition, Santi Parva section CCC), with footnotes drawing on Nilakantha
commentaries.gist: The righteous person who, joyful and free of malice, subdues the blazing wrath that, if indulged, would make him speak ill and become an enemy, takes away the merit of others.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition text (12.288) as a textual check
commentaries.gist: Same wording in the critical text (12.288.11); 12.288.12 follows with the swan's own example of forgiving abuse and blows.

practical_reading: When anger flares after a slight, notice the heat, breathe, and decide not to let it poison how you see the person.
misreadings: Not 'never feel anger'; it is about holding back the blaze and keeping the heart clean.
cautions: Same caution as 12.288.10 for people facing repeated mistreatment.
not_for: someone in an abusive relationship

attribution_note: Speaker is the Swan, who in 12.288.3 is Prajapati (the unborn, eternal creator) in the form of a golden swan; listeners are the Sadhya gods. Bhishma narrates to Yudhishthira.

key_terms.sense: though addressed harshly, says nothing harsh or flattering in return
struck, does not strike back, out of steadiness

key_terms.term: pāpaṃ ca yo necchati tasya hantuḥ
key_terms.sense: and wishes no harm to the one who struck

core_teaching: The highest steadiness is not just restraining retaliation but not even wishing harm on the one who hurt you.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli's translation (P. C. Roy edition, Santi Parva section CCC), with footnotes drawing on Nilakantha
commentaries.gist: One who answers harsh words with no harsh word, does not flatter back when praised, and has the fortitude neither to strike back nor wish the striker evil, finds his company always sought by the gods.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition text (12.288) as a textual check
commentaries.gist: Critical text 12.288.17 has the same wording; the swan frames it as a description of a character the gods desire, not as a command.

practical_reading: Notice the urge to get even, even in thought; let it pass without feeding it.
misreadings: Not 'do nothing when harmed'; it is about non-retaliation and not wishing harm, not about refusing protection or justice.
cautions: For someone who has been assaulted, 'when struck does not strike back' must never be framed as a duty; this is an ideal of character, not instruction to a victim.
not_for: victims of violence or assault
anyone being told to forgive too soon

key_terms.sense: the steady one succeeds through patience

core_teaching: Freed from wrongdoing, the steady person waits patiently for the right time, and through that patience reaches fulfilment.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli's translation (P. C. Roy edition, Santi Parva section CCC), with footnotes drawing on Nilakantha
commentaries.gist: Freed from sin like the moon from murky clouds, the wise man, shining, attains success by patiently waiting for his time. Ganguli places it right after the line that no status is higher than humanity.

misreadings: Not 'wait passively for luck'; the patience follows self-purification and restraint.

The critical text reads 'abudhād vardhate budhaḥ' (from abuse and insult by a fool, the wise one grows). The second line is the same in both. Our English is faithful to our Sanskrit.
context: Part of the swan's teaching on speech: revilers are keener to talk of a person's faults than of his virtues (12.288.23); the one whose speech and mind are guarded gains everything (12.288.24). This verse then tells the wise not to answer abuse with abuse.

key_terms.sense: should not inflame (or exalt) the other

core_teaching: Answering insult with insult feeds the other's anger and damages you; the wise reply is restraint.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli's translation (P. C. Roy edition, Santi Parva section CCC), with footnotes drawing on Nilakantha
commentaries.gist: The wise should never revile the undeserving in return with dispraise and insult; he should not extol others (merely because they extol him), and should never injure himself.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition text (12.288) as a textual check
commentaries.gist: Critical text 12.288.25 reads differently in its first line: a wise person grows (in merit) through the abuse he receives from a fool; therefore he should not make the other grow (in anger) nor harm himself.

practical_reading: Before replying to a rude person, ask whether the reply will cool things or heat them, and whether it will cost you your own peace.
misreadings: It governs your reply, not whether to accept mistreatment (our_note says this well).
cautions: 'The ignorant' can sound contemptuous; better framed as 'someone acting without understanding'.

key_terms.sense: should be as satisfied as with nectar
the one insulted sleeps at ease
the one who insults comes to ruin

core_teaching: Insult need not disturb the one who receives it; the real damage falls on the one who gives it.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli's translation (P. C. Roy edition, Santi Parva section CCC), with footnotes drawing on Nilakantha
commentaries.gist: The wise and learned man regards revilement as nectar; reviled, he sleeps without anxiety, while the reviler meets with destruction.

commentaries.who: Medhatithi on Manusmriti 2.162-163 (parallel verse; trans. Ganganath Jha)
commentaries.gist: Explains the parallel: the point is to look equally on respect and disrespect, not actually to hanker after disrespect. One unperturbed by scorn sleeps and wakes in comfort; otherwise he would burn with resentment.

practical_reading: If an insult replays at night, remind yourself the injury is theirs to carry; you can let it go and sleep.

cautions: For a reader being humiliated at home or work, 'be satisfied by insult as by nectar' can sound like endorsement of mistreatment; use Medhatithi's framing (equanimity, not appetite for disrespect).

children being bullied

core_teaching: Wisdom shows as quiet contentment, the ability to stay silent in a crowd, inner strength without outer power, and staying out of quarrels.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli's translation (P. C. Roy edition, Santi Parva section CCC), with footnotes drawing on Nilakantha
commentaries.gist: Only the brahmana possessed of wisdom is always happy, can keep silence while living among many, is regarded as strong though actually weak, and avoids quarrels. Footnote (Nilakantha): the verse shows the merits of one whose ignorance has gone.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition text (12.288) as a textual check
commentaries.gist: Same wording in the critical text (12.288.42); the question at 288.41 names 'among brahmanas'.

practical_reading: In a heated group chat or meeting, practise being the one who does not need to join the fight.
misreadings: Not that silence is always right; it is about not being dragged into quarrels.
not_for: someone who needs to speak up against wrongdoing and might hear 'stay quiet'

verified_ref: Adhyatma Ramayana, Uttara Kanda, sarga 5 (the Rama Gita), verse 5. Same number in the Gita Press edition and in Baij Nath's 1913 translation.
attribution_note: Speaker Lakshmana, listener Rama: correct. Our data spells them 'Lakshman'/'Ram' here and in 61 but 'Lakshmana'/'Rama' elsewhere; make consistent. Setting 'alone with Ram' is close: verse 3 says Rama sat in seclusion while Sita (as Lakshmi) pressed his feet. Within the Adhyatma Ramayana the whole Rama Gita is narrated by Mahadeva (Shiva) to Parvati.
context: After the coronation, Rama tells Lakshmana old stories of dharma (sarga 5.2). Lakshmana, his mind purified by devotion, finds Rama in seclusion, bows, praises him as pure knowledge (5.4) and makes this request. Rama, pleased, begins the teaching at 5.6-7 with the steps that lead to a teacher.
core_teaching: The teaching begins with a humble request: refuge first, then the ask to be taught a simple way across confusion.

commentaries.who: Rai Bahadur Lala Baij Nath, Adhyatma Ramayana translation with notes (1913) (translation reading)
commentaries.gist: Lakshmana takes refuge in Rama's feet, which free one from worldly life and which yogis cherish, and asks for the knowledge to cross the impassable ocean of nescience quickly and easily.

commentaries.who: Gita Press Adhyatma Ramayana, Hindi translation (numbering check)
commentaries.gist: Same verse number and wording; immediately followed by Rama, 'remover of the distress of those who take refuge', answering with knowledge to dispel ignorance.

practical_reading: Asking for help is itself the first step; name the confusion and ask someone wiser to show you a way through.
misreadings: Not passivity; the request leads straight into a demanding discipline.
cautions: Within the Adhyatma Ramayana the whole Rama Gita is narrated by Mahadeva (Shiva) to Parvati.
research_note: No separate commentary note on this verse in Baij Nath; the Nepali tika's gloss for this verse was not legible in the OCR.

verified_ref: Adhyatma Ramayana, Uttara Kanda, sarga 5 (the Rama Gita), verse 24 in Baij Nath's 1913 translation (Gita Press numbering agrees for the neighbouring verses checked).
attribution_note: Within the Adhyatma Ramayana the whole Rama Gita is narrated by Mahadeva (Shiva) to Parvati.
context: Rama has argued (5.7-23) that ritual action cannot remove ignorance and that knowledge alone frees; that the duties of one's station purify the mind first. Here he names the means: faith, the teacher's grace and the great saying 'tat tvam asi'. Verses 25-27 then explain how the words That and Thou are understood.

key_terms.sense: oneness of the supreme Self and the individual

core_teaching: Faith, a pure mind and a teacher's grace, applied to the teaching that you are one with the Self, make a person happy and as unshakable as a mountain.

commentaries.who: Rai Bahadur Lala Baij Nath, Adhyatma Ramayana translation with notes (1913)
commentaries.gist: Stresses that the unity taught by 'That art thou' is realised through a guru's grace and personal contact, not mere verbal teaching; notes that such teachers are rare, which is why many read Vedanta and few realise it.

commentaries.who: Anonymous Sanskrit tika in a Nepali printed Rama Gita (commentator not named in the scan)
commentaries.gist: Glosses 'unshakable' as having an inner organ no longer agitated by craving for sense objects.

practical_reading: Steadiness grows from three things together: trust, good guidance and a clear understanding of who you are; check which of the three is missing.
misreadings: Not a promise of instant calm by repeating a phrase; the commentators insist on preparation and a teacher.
cautions: Advaita identity claims can feel abstract; best paired with the image of the mountain rather than the doctrine.

verified_ref: Adhyatma Ramayana, Uttara Kanda, sarga 5 (the Rama Gita), verse 34. Same number in the Gita Press edition and in Baij Nath's 1913 translation.
attribution_note: Within the Adhyatma Ramayana the whole Rama Gita is narrated by Mahadeva (Shiva) to Parvati.
translation_note: The 'coconut' is supported by the Sanskrit tika, which gives coconut and orange as examples of a fruit whose juice is drunk and whose rest is left. Baij Nath has just 'a fruit after sucking off the juice'.
context: Rama has explained the gross, subtle and causal bodies and the three states, all of which belong to the intellect, not the Self (5.28-33). Here he gives the method: negate everything with 'not this, not this', taste the Self, then let the world go. Verse 35 states what the Self is.

key_terms.sense: by the means of 'not this, not this'
having drunk the water, one discards the fruit

core_teaching: Once one has tasted the Self by negating what one is not, the world can be let go the way one sets down a fruit after drinking its juice.

commentaries.who: Rai Bahadur Lala Baij Nath, Adhyatma Ramayana translation with notes (1913)
commentaries.gist: Notes that for one who has reached realisation through neti neti, the world ceases to assert itself and he becomes indifferent to its joys and sorrows; but this is the state of the jivanmukta, not of everyone.

commentaries.who: Anonymous Sanskrit tika in a Nepali printed Rama Gita (commentator not named in the scan)
commentaries.gist: Answers the objection that the world is enjoyed: as with a coconut or orange, one drinks the sweet juice and leaves the rest; once the essence is taken, the remainder is dropped, since it brings fear.

practical_reading: In a smaller key: take what is nourishing from an experience, a job, even a relationship that has ended, and let the husk go without bitterness.
misreadings: Not 'the world is worthless, discard people'; Baij Nath limits it to the jivanmukta's inner detachment.
Not a call to quit responsibilities.
cautions: For someone who feels used and discarded by others, the 'shell' image could sting; avoid in breakup or abandonment contexts.
speaks_to: letting go after a chapter ends
not_for: someone who has just been left or let go
depression with withdrawal from life

verified_ref: Adhyatma Ramayana, Uttara Kanda, sarga 5 (the Rama Gita), verse 35. Same number in the Gita Press edition and in Baij Nath's 1913 translation.
attribution_note: Within the Adhyatma Ramayana the whole Rama Gita is narrated by Mahadeva (Shiva) to Parvati.
translation_note: 'Ancient' for anavaḥ is defensible; the Sanskrit tika reads a-navaḥ as 'not new', i.e. without the coming-into-being that follows birth.
context: Follows the neti neti method (5.34). The next verse asks: if the Self is such, how does a sorrowful world appear in it? Answer: through ignorance and superimposition, which knowledge removes in a moment (5.36); 5.37 defines superimposition.
core_teaching: What you truly are is untouched by the changes of birth, growth, decline and death: whole, self-luminous and one.

commentaries.who: Rai Bahadur Lala Baij Nath, Adhyatma Ramayana translation with notes (1913)
commentaries.gist: The embodied self, taken to be subject to birth and death, is not subject to any of them; free of them it is the limitless Brahman itself, as the Upanishadic saying 'this Self is Brahman' declares.

commentaries.who: Anonymous Sanskrit tika in a Nepali printed Rama Gita (commentator not named in the scan)
commentaries.gist: Reads the verse as denying all six modifications of things (to exist, be born, grow, change, decline, perish), so that the Self alone is eternal; quotes 'ayam ātmā brahma'.

practical_reading: In times of change (ageing, illness, a move), some teachers suggest resting attention on the awareness that has watched every change and is still here.
misreadings: Not a denial that bodies age and die, or that loss hurts.
cautions: Restates Gita 2.20's theme of the deathless Self; can feel dismissive to fresh grief if offered as consolation for a death.
speaks_to: fear of ageing or death in reflective moments
not_for: fresh bereavement
terminal diagnosis without pastoral care
research_note: Our_note's parallels (Gita 2.20, Katha 1.2.18) are standard; not re-checked in this run.

verified_ref: Adhyatma Ramayana, Uttara Kanda, sarga 5 (the Rama Gita), verse 37. Same number in the Gita Press edition and in Baij Nath's 1913 translation.
attribution_note: Within the Adhyatma Ramayana the whole Rama Gita is narrated by Mahadeva (Shiva) to Parvati.
context: After saying the world appears in the blissful Self only through ignorance (5.36), Rama defines superimposition with the rope-snake example. Verse 38 adds that the first superimposition is the notion 'I' on the Self, and 39 turns to deep sleep as evidence.

key_terms.sense: superimposition: seeing one thing as another

core_teaching: Suffering comes from mistaking one thing for another, like a rope for a snake; the world and the 'I' are laid over the one reality by confusion.

commentaries.who: Rai Bahadur Lala Baij Nath, Adhyatma Ramayana translation with notes (1913) (translation and surrounding notes)
commentaries.gist: Superimposition is what is imposed on another thing through illusion, as a rope is taken for a snake; so the world is laid on the Lord, and the Self is taken to be happy, miserable, born and dying.

commentaries.who: Anonymous Sanskrit tika in a Nepali printed Rama Gita (commentator not named in the scan)
commentaries.gist: Introduces the next verse as saying the first superimposition is ego (ahaṅkāra) on the Self, the cause of all saṃsāra; and earlier compares the disappearance of the world on knowledge to the snake vanishing when the rope is seen.

practical_reading: When fear or anger spikes, pause and look again; much of what frightens us is a rope taken for a snake.
misreadings: Not 'your problems are imaginary'; it is about seeing clearly, which may still call for action.
cautions: Telling someone in real danger that it is 'just a rope' would be harmful; keep it to misperception and anxiety.
not_for: real threats or trauma
research_note: Our_note's link to Shankara's adhyasa-bhashya is a fair scholarly observation but not checked here.

verified_ref: Adhyatma Ramayana, Uttara Kanda, sarga 5 (the Rama Gita), verse 39. Same number in the Gita Press edition and in Baij Nath's 1913 translation.
attribution_note: Within the Adhyatma Ramayana the whole Rama Gita is narrated by Mahadeva (Shiva) to Parvati.
context: After defining superimposition (5.37-38), Rama gives the evidence of deep sleep: the mind's states cease there and the Self is experienced as happiness. 5.40-41 then explain how consciousness and intellect seem to borrow each other's qualities, like fire and iron.

key_terms.sense: desire and the like, attachment and the like, pleasure and the like (each with its opposite)
properties of the intellect, not of the Self
as the very form of happiness

core_teaching: Wanting, clinging and even pleasure and pain belong to the mind; in dreamless sleep they stop and we are simply at ease, which hints that ease is our nature.

commentaries.who: Rai Bahadur Lala Baij Nath, Adhyatma Ramayana translation with notes (1913)
commentaries.gist: Explains the pairs: desire and aversion, attachment and non-attachment, happiness and misery are states of the intellect, which vanish in deep sleep when the Self is known as bliss; cites the Brihadaranyaka's description of deep sleep.

commentaries.who: Gita Press Adhyatma Ramayana, Hindi translation (numbering check)
commentaries.gist: Same verse number; the Hindi rendering stresses that these are properties of the intellect and the cause of saṃsāra, absent in deep sleep.

practical_reading: Notice how a good night's sleep resets you even though nothing outside changed; ease does not always need new things.
misreadings: Not an argument that unconsciousness is the goal.
cautions: For readers with insomnia, avoid making sleep sound like the measure of spiritual health.
not_for: chronic insomnia sufferers as the main hook
research_note: Sanskrit tika for this verse was not legible in the OCR.

verified_ref: Adhyatma Ramayana, Uttara Kanda, sarga 5 (the Rama Gita), verse 46. Same number in the Gita Press edition and in Baij Nath's 1913 translation.
attribution_note: Within the Adhyatma Ramayana the whole Rama Gita is narrated by Mahadeva (Shiva) to Parvati.
context: After the 'I am' contemplations of 5.43-44 and the image of a sick man cured by an elixir (5.45), Rama gives the posture of meditation. 5.47-51 then describe merging the universe into the Self and meditating on Om (A, U, M).
core_teaching: Sit apart, quiet the senses, steady the mind and contemplate the one Self with undivided attention.

commentaries.who: Rai Bahadur Lala Baij Nath, Adhyatma Ramayana translation with notes (1913)
commentaries.gist: Uses the verse to set out the seven stages of yoga (right desire, right thought, non-attachment, purity, non-cognition of objects, turiya, beyond turiya), adding that in his day few pass the third stage.

commentaries.who: Anonymous Sanskrit tika in a Nepali printed Rama Gita (commentator not named in the scan)
commentaries.gist: Reads it as nirvikalpa samadhi; 'no other means' means free of the error that anything besides knowledge of truth liberates; 'kevala' is unattached; the mind never strays to another object.

practical_reading: A plain meditation instruction: a quiet corner, phone away, a few minutes of resting attention on awareness itself.
misreadings: Not a demand to leave family for a cave; a 'secluded place' can be a quiet room.
not_for: people with trauma for whom unguided silent sitting can be destabilising

verified_ref: Adhyatma Ramayana, Uttara Kanda, sarga 5 (the Rama Gita), verse 52. Same number in the Gita Press edition and in Baij Nath's 1913 translation.
attribution_note: Within the Adhyatma Ramayana the whole Rama Gita is narrated by Mahadeva (Shiva) to Parvati.
context: After the Om meditation that merges gross, subtle and causal into pure awareness (5.48-51), Rama describes the result. 5.53 says such a yogi sees him; 5.54 says he lives on until his past karma is spent and then merges in Rama.

key_terms.sense: in whom the sense of the supreme Self has arisen
like an ocean of still water

core_teaching: The freed person rests content in the Self's own joy, free and still like a waveless ocean.

commentaries.who: Rai Bahadur Lala Baij Nath, Adhyatma Ramayana translation with notes (1913)
commentaries.gist: This is the state where the mind has merged in the Self; not a void or nothingness but something very real, beside which what now seems real looks unreal; the goal of all religion.

commentaries.who: Anonymous Sanskrit tika in a Nepali printed Rama Gita (commentator not named in the scan)
commentaries.gist: Glosses 'still ocean' as one whose waters have no waves of contact with sense objects; such a one is liberated while living.

practical_reading: An image to rest in: beneath surface waves the ocean is still; on busy days return to that stillness for a few breaths.
misreadings: 'Forgetting all else' is not neglecting people or duties; it describes absorption.
cautions: Describes an advanced state; avoid making a struggling reader feel they are failing.

verified_ref: Adhyatma Ramayana, Uttara Kanda, sarga 5 (the Rama Gita), verse 58. Same number in the Gita Press edition and in Baij Nath's 1913 translation.
attribution_note: Within the Adhyatma Ramayana the whole Rama Gita is narrated by Mahadeva (Shiva) to Parvati.
context: After the austere path of knowledge and samadhi (5.46-57), Rama adds that until one sees everything as himself, one should be devoted to worshipping him. He then says this teaching is the essence of the Vedas (5.59) and that he purifies those who serve him (5.61).

key_terms.sense: as long as one does not see all as Me
I am seen in the heart day and night

core_teaching: Knowledge and devotion are joined: keep worshipping until you see the divine everywhere, and to the faithful the divine is present in the heart day and night.

commentaries.who: Rai Bahadur Lala Baij Nath, Adhyatma Ramayana translation with notes (1913)
commentaries.gist: Rama here reveals that the secret of knowledge lies in uninterrupted devotion; those who seek the goal by knowledge alone find it hard, while for the devotee the Lord removes obstacles unnoticed, as for Prahlada, Bhishma, Vyasa and Narada.

commentaries.who: Anonymous Sanskrit tika in a Nepali printed Rama Gita (commentator not named in the scan)
commentaries.gist: Links it to Gita 4.11, 'as people approach me, so I receive them': the faithful worshipper sees the Lord in the heart day and night.

practical_reading: Keep a daily practice of love and attention, even a small one, while understanding grows.
misreadings: Not that worship is only for beginners to discard later; Baij Nath presents devotion as the secret of knowledge.

verified_ref: Adhyatma Ramayana, Uttara Kanda, sarga 5 (the Rama Gita), verse 61. Same number in the Gita Press edition and in Baij Nath's 1913 translation.
attribution_note: Speaker Rama, listener Lakshmana (spelled 'Ram'/'Lakshman' in our data; make consistent). This is not quite the close: 5.62 follows, saying that whoever reads this teaching with faith and devotion to the guru attains Rama's form. Within the Adhyatma Ramayana the whole Rama Gita is narrated by Mahadeva (Shiva) to Parvati.
translation_note: 'Now and then' (kadā vā) is supported: the tika reads it as 'whenever, at any time'. 'Becomes me' (so 'ham) is the plain sense; Baij Nath: becomes my own self.
context: After telling Lakshmana that the visible world is maya and he should purify his mind by meditating on Rama (5.60), Rama makes this promise. The chapter ends with 5.62 on the merit of reading the Rama Gita.

key_terms.sense: in the heart, at whatever time
with the dust of his feet

core_teaching: Whether one worships the divine as formless or with form, even sometimes, sincere inner worship makes one one with Rama and a source of blessing to the world.

commentaries.who: Rai Bahadur Lala Baij Nath, Adhyatma Ramayana translation with notes (1913)
commentaries.gist: Contemplation with attributes and without attributes leads to the same goal, one leading into the other; the devotee merges into the knower, as Bhishma and Prahlada did through the Lord with attributes.

commentaries.who: Anonymous Sanskrit tika in a Nepali printed Rama Gita (commentator not named in the scan)
commentaries.gist: 'With a pure heart, at any time'; aguṇa because free of nature's three qualities, being being-consciousness-bliss; guṇātmaka as having omniscience and beauty beyond the world. Either kind of worshipper becomes Rama's own form.

practical_reading: Reassurance for the irregular practitioner: sincere remembrance, even occasional, counts.
misreadings: Not that occasional practice makes discipline unnecessary; 'pure heart' is the condition.
cautions: Within the Adhyatma Ramayana the whole Rama Gita is narrated by Mahadeva (Shiva) to Parvati.
speaks_to: people who pray irregularly and feel guilty
debates about form vs formless worship

verified_ref: Shakti Gita 1.42-43 in the Mahamandal editions read (1916 and 1957 agree; 1.40 there is the speaker line 'the gods said'). Our '1.39-40' is off by three. The printed Mahamandal editions number speaker lines ('devā ūcuḥ ॥1॥' etc.) as verses, so their numbers run ahead of ours.
translation_note: Sanskrit in our data has OCR errors: 'विमोदिता' should be 'विमोहिता' (deluded/carried away), 'वांगमनोधियाम' should be 'वाङ्मनोधियाम्', and 'तवां' should be 'त्वां'. The English follows the correct sense.
context: After winning the war with the demons, the gods, led by Vishnu, perform a collective worship (the 'brahma-chakra') hoping the Mother will appear. She appears as a blazing light and a radiant sixteen-year-old form. The gods begin a hymn by admitting that no one can praise her in words (1.41), then ask pardon for trying (1.42-43).

key_terms.sense: carried away by the rush of the mind
beyond the reach of speech, mind and intellect

core_teaching: Every attempt to praise the divine falls short, and even being forgiven for that is itself grace; the right response is grateful bowing.

commentaries.who: Bharat Dharma Mahamandal Hindi bhashanuvada (publisher's own Hindi rendering, 1957 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Moved by emotion, the gods tried to put into words what lies beyond speech, mind and thought, and ask forgiveness; only her vast compassion makes that forgiveness possible. They bow to the compassionate Mother of the world.

commentaries.who: Devi Anugraha Foundation English translation (recent; text and readings unreliable)
commentaries.gist: Prints a different and garbled second verse (e.g. 'moonlight of the world'); useful only as evidence that the text circulates in variant forms. Not used for meaning.

practical_reading: Permission to pray clumsily: words will not be enough, and that is fine; the intention is received.
cautions: One of five sectarian Gitas (Vishnu, Surya, Shakti, Dhisha, Shambhu) issued with Hindi translation by the Bharat Dharma Mahamandal, Kashi, in the early 20th century; the Mahamandal's own preface calls them previously unpublished. No classical commentary or older manuscript tradition was found; date and authorship unverified.
speaks_to: people who feel they do not know how to pray

verified_ref: Shakti Gita 1.50-51 in the Mahamandal editions (1916 and 1957 agree). Our '1.47-48' is off by three. The printed Mahamandal editions number speaker lines ('devā ūcuḥ ॥1॥' etc.) as verses, so their numbers run ahead of ours.
translation_note: Minor: the Hindi rendering takes guṇāśrayāt as 'by taking on qualities (a form)', i.e. she shows herself in a qualified form; our English drops this. Sanskrit typo: 'गुणाश्रयायच्छसि' should be 'गुणाश्रयाद्यच्छसि'.
context: Part of the gods' hymn. Just before (1.48-49) they say she, though formless and beyond the senses, takes a form with qualities for her devotees' good. Just after (1.52-54) they say not even gods understand her, yet she does not withhold her vision from simple devotees who love her feet.
core_teaching: Grace does not wait for perfect understanding: to devotees who cannot yet see her true nature, the Mother shows herself in a form and gives both well-being and freedom.

commentaries.who: Bharat Dharma Mahamandal Hindi bhashanuvada (publisher's own Hindi rendering, 1957 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Her grace has no limit: to the devotee who, lacking full knowledge, cannot see her true form, she out of natural compassion shows herself in a form with qualities and grants both worldly good and liberation.

practical_reading: You do not have to understand everything to be helped; begin where you are.
misreadings: Not anti-knowledge; the hymn values understanding but says grace is wider.
cautions: One of five sectarian Gitas (Vishnu, Surya, Shakti, Dhisha, Shambhu) issued with Hindi translation by the Bharat Dharma Mahamandal, Kashi, in the early 20th century; the Mahamandal's own preface calls them previously unpublished. No classical commentary or older manuscript tradition was found; date and authorship unverified.

verified_ref: Shakti Gita 1.54 in the 1957 Mahamandal edition. Our '1.51' is off by three. The printed Mahamandal editions number speaker lines ('devā ūcuḥ ॥1॥' etc.) as verses, so their numbers run ahead of ours.
translation_note: Sanskrit typos: 'अनन्यभक्सैव' should be 'अनन्यभक्त्यैव'; 'पादपद्यमे' should be 'पादपद्मे'. The verse is one sentence with 1.53, which says these devotees are ignorant and do not grasp her greatness; our English could say 'even those who do not understand'.
context: The gods say (1.53) that her devotees, bound by ignorance, do not understand her greatness at all; yet (1.54) those who love her feet with undivided devotion like bees are never turned away from the vision that gives freedom. 1.55 adds that she appears to each in whichever of the five deity forms (Vishnu, Surya, Gauri, Dhisha, Shiva) they like.

key_terms.sense: you do not let (them) slip away

core_teaching: Simple, single-minded love is enough: the Mother does not withhold herself from devotees who cling to her like bees to a lotus, even if they understand little.

commentaries.who: Bharat Dharma Mahamandal Hindi bhashanuvada (publisher's own Hindi rendering, 1957 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Even the devotee bound by ignorance, who grasps nothing of her greatness but loves her feet like a bee with undivided devotion, is not kept from her liberating vision; she appears in the form he prefers.

practical_reading: Devotion does not require theology; keep returning, like a bee, to what you love in prayer.
cautions: One of five sectarian Gitas (Vishnu, Surya, Shakti, Dhisha, Shambhu) issued with Hindi translation by the Bharat Dharma Mahamandal, Kashi, in the early 20th century; the Mahamandal's own preface calls them previously unpublished. No classical commentary or older manuscript tradition was found; date and authorship unverified.
speaks_to: people who feel they lack learning

verified_ref: Shakti Gita 5.135 in the 1957 Mahamandal edition (the Devi Anugraha English also numbers it 135). Our '5.133' is off by two.
translation_note: Sanskrit typos: 'गृणीता' should be 'गृह्णीत', 'मयुक्ताः कुरुतामराः' should be 'मद्युक्ताः कुरुतामराः'.
context: In a chapter on karma, the Mother tells the gods to work joined to her. The next verse explains why: action done without union with her binds, action done joined to her gives the highest freedom (5.136). Then: the world arises from the push and pull of opposites, and her shelter is what lifts one beyond them (5.137-139).

key_terms.sense: devotion to Me as the highest goal

core_teaching: Keep doing your work, but do it held in the divine, as shelter and goal; that changes the work from binding to freeing.

commentaries.who: Bharat Dharma Mahamandal Hindi bhashanuvada (publisher's own Hindi rendering, 1957 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Hindi rendering: be devoted to her, take her shelter, and as her devotees always act with minds joined to her; the next verse explains that work done apart from her binds, while work done joined to her gives liberation.

practical_reading: Before a task, offer it; during it, return to that offering when you notice stress.
misreadings: Not quietism: the Mother explicitly says to keep working.
cautions: One of five sectarian Gitas (Vishnu, Surya, Shakti, Dhisha, Shambhu) issued with Hindi translation by the Bharat Dharma Mahamandal, Kashi, in the early 20th century; the Mahamandal's own preface calls them previously unpublished. No classical commentary or older manuscript tradition was found; date and authorship unverified.
research_note: Only one sourced note exists. Our_note's Gita parallels (8.7, 18.57) were not re-verified.

verified_ref: Shakti Gita 5.139 in the 1957 Mahamandal edition (Devi Anugraha English also 139). Our '5.137' is off by two.
translation_note: The sentence continues into 5.140: such devotees, when they also become vowed to desireless action, become fit for liberation. Our English is accurate for this verse but reads as a complete thought; consider adding 5.140. Also 'तदाश्रयेण' refers to 'that one principle' (ekatattva, 5.138), which the Hindi identifies as the cause of release, not directly to 5.133's shelter.
context: The Mother explains (5.137-138) that the world arises and stays through the push and pull of opposites, which bind beings, but one principle frees them. Relying on it, devotees go beyond the pairs and envy (5.139) and, practising desireless action, become fit for liberation (5.140); karmic seeds are then burned (5.141).
core_teaching: Relying on the divine lifts a person above the swing of opposites and envy, into steady, fitting work, and prepares them for freedom.

commentaries.who: Bharat Dharma Mahamandal Hindi bhashanuvada (publisher's own Hindi rendering, 1957 ed.)
commentaries.gist: The world is born of attraction and repulsion between opposites, which bind; one principle releases. Relying on it, devotees go beyond opposites and envy, do fitting work, become sinless and, vowed to desireless action, fit for liberation.

practical_reading: When comparison and envy pull at you, return to your own fitting work and your refuge.

translation_note: Sanskrit has OCR noise: 'अमनस्कस्यं' should be 'अमनस्कस्य' and 'संकल्पान' 'सङ्कल्पान्'; the first word is unclear in the scan read (perhaps 'समनस्कानां'), so check a clean copy. verified_ref: Vishnu Gita 1.61 in the 1919 Mahamandal edition. Our '1.58' is off by three.
translation_note: Sanskrit typo: 'आपि' should be 'अपि'. Important context: the very next verse (1.62) says the Lord removes the delusion of those who forget him by 'the discipline of calamity' (vipat-śāsana), and calls that great mercy.
context: The frightened gods praise Vishnu as the one whose power moves them (1.60). Here they confess that they exist only by his being, yet forget him through maya (1.61). core_teaching: We exist only because the divine exists, yet we forget it; that forgetting, not the divine's absence, is the root of our fear.

practical_reading: A remembering practice: before a fearful task, recall what holds your existence before you recall what threatens it.
cautions: One of five sectarian Gitas (Vishnu, Surya, Shakti, Dhisha, Shambhu) issued with Hindi translation by the Bharat Dharma Mahamandal, Kashi, in the early 20th century; the Mahamandal's own preface calls them previously unpublished.
